# Absorption, spontaneous and stimulated emission {#sec-einstein} [![Open in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/{{< var github_user >}}/{{< var repo >}}/blob/main/{{< var subdir >}}/notebooks/einstein.ipynb){.colab-link}  Run this chapter's code in Google Colab (no installation). *Slides 8–10 (spontaneous versus stimulated emission, the three decay channels of an excited electron) and 15–19 (Einstein coefficients, laser requirements, spontaneous decay time).* ## Key relations Three processes connect two levels $E_1steady state: N₂/N₀ = ${tlOut.ss.toFixed(4)}, N₂/N₁ = ${(tlOut.ss/(1 - tlOut.ss)).toFixed(4)} < 1 · the medium ${tlOut.ss > 0.45 ? "is saturated (transparent) but never amplifies" : "still absorbs"}` ``` At most the medium becomes **transparent** ($N_2\to N_1$). This is why the ruby laser needs a third level and why the semiconductor laser needs electrical injection (@sec-pumping, @sec-ld-principle). ## From lifetime to Einstein coefficients The spontaneous lifetime is the measured quantity. The $B$ coefficient follows from $A_{21}/B_{21}$. The ratio grows as $\nu^3$: at short wavelengths spontaneous emission becomes fast and steals the inversion. This is one reason why the first stimulated-emission device was a microwave **maser** (1954), and why X-ray lasers are so hard. ::: {#tbl-ab .cell tbl-cap='Spontaneous lifetimes of laser transitions used in this chapter, and the Einstein B21 coefficient that follows from A21/B21 = 8πhν³n³/c³.' execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} trans = [("Cr³⁺:Al₂O₃ (ruby), slide 13", 694.3e-9, 3e-3, 1.76), ("Nd³⁺:YAG, slide 14", 1064e-9, 230e-6, 1.82), ("Er³⁺:silica (EDFA), slide 39", 1550e-9, 10e-3, 1.45), ("Ne (He–Ne), slide 69", 632.8e-9, 100e-9, 1.0), ("GaAs band-to-band (2e18 cm⁻³)", 870e-9, 2.5e-9, 3.6)] rows = [] for name, wl, tau, n in trans: nu = lz.c0/wl rows.append({"transition": name, "λ (nm)": round(wl*1e9, 1), "τ_sp": f"{tau:.3g} s", "n": n, "A21 (s⁻¹)": f"{1/tau:.3g}", "B21 (m³ J⁻¹ s⁻²)": f"{1/tau/lz.A_over_B(nu, n):.3g}"}) pd.DataFrame(rows) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Long-lived (metastable) levels such as those of Cr³⁺ and Er³⁺ store energy for milliseconds. This makes inversion easy with modest pumps, and it makes these media good **energy stores** for Q-switching (@sec-pulsed). Semiconductors recombine in nanoseconds: they need large current densities but can be modulated at GHz rates (@sec-modulation). ## Stimulated versus spontaneous emission: the cavity In thermal equilibrium the ratio stimulated/spontaneous is $1/(e^{h\nu/k_BT}-1)$, about $10^{-33}$ for red light at 300 K (@sec-blackbody). A cavity traps the emitted photons and raises $\rho(\nu)$ in a few modes by many orders of magnitude. The figure shows the photon density needed for stimulated emission to win: ::: {#cell-fig-stimspont .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} nu, dnu = lz.c0/632.8e-9, 1.5e9 Nph = np.logspace(10, 20, 200) rho = Nph*lz.h*nu/dnu ratio = rho/lz.A_over_B(nu) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.6)) ax.loglog(Nph, ratio) ax.axhline(1, color=lz.INK2, ls="--", lw=1.2); ax.axvline(2.1e15, color=lz.PALETTE[1], lw=1.2) ax.text(2.4e15, 1e-4, "He–Ne laser\n(slide 73)", fontsize=8, color=lz.PALETTE[1]) ax.set(xlabel="photon density N_ph (m⁻³)", ylabel="R(stim)/R(spon) per atom"); plt.show() print(f"stimulated = spontaneous at N_ph = {lz.A_over_B(nu)*dnu/(lz.h*nu):.2e} m^-3") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Ratio of stimulated to spontaneous emission rates, c³ρ(ν)/(8πhν³), versus photon density in the mode volume for a transition at 632.8 nm with a 1.5 GHz linewidth (ρ ≈ N_ph hν/Δν, slide 64). Inside a He–Ne laser N_ph ≈ 2×10¹⁵ m⁻³ (slide 73).](einstein_files/figure-html/fig-stimspont-output-1.png){#fig-stimspont width=705 height=376} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` stimulated = spontaneous at N_ph = 3.14e+14 m^-3 ``` ::: ::: Inside the He–Ne laser the ratio is about 7: thanks to the mirrors, stimulated emission wins. The ratio $c^3\rho/8\pi h\nu^3$ is the **number of photons per mode**: $N_\text{ph}$ divided by the number of modes per unit volume within the linewidth, $8\pi\nu^2\Delta\nu/c^3=3\times10^{14}$ m⁻³. The cavity does not fill every mode. It selects one (or a few) modes and lets the photons pile up there. The spontaneous emission into all the other modes is lost: it limits the efficiency and adds noise (@sec-linewidth). ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Going further - **Degenerate levels.** If $E_1$ and $E_2$ have degeneracies $g_1$, $g_2$, detailed balance gives $g_1B_{12}=g_2B_{21}$ and the inversion condition becomes $N_2/g_2>N_1/g_1$. Redo the derivation of slide 16 with degeneracies. - **From $A_{21}$ to a cross section.** For a transition with a normalised lineshape $g(\nu)$, the emission cross section is $\sigma_{em}(\nu)=\dfrac{\lambda^2}{8\pi n^2\tau_{sp}}g(\nu)$ (Füchtbauer–Ladenburg). Check the order of magnitude of the Er³⁺ value used in @sec-edfa: $\lambda=1.53$ µm, $\tau_{sp}=10$ ms, $\Delta\nu\approx4$ THz. - **Which $B$?** Some books define $B$ with the intensity $I$, the photon flux or the angular frequency instead of $\rho(\nu)$. The numerical values differ by $c/n$, $h\nu$ or $2\pi$. Always check the definition before using a tabulated value. - **Non-radiative channels** (slide 10). Multiphonon emission depends on how many phonons bridge the gap $E_2-E_1$. This "energy-gap law" explains why the Er³⁺ $^4I_{13/2}$ level (0.8 eV) is long-lived in silica but the $^4I_{11/2}$ pump level decays in microseconds. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Complements - A. Einstein, "Zur Quantentheorie der Strahlung", *Physikalische Zeitschrift* 18, 121 (1917): the original argument. - Kasap, sec. 4.1–4.2; Svelto, *Principles of Lasers*, 5th ed., ch. 2. - R. Loudon, *The Quantum Theory of Light*, ch. 1–2: why stimulated photons are identical. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. From the rate equation of the two-level panel, derive the 1/e time to reach the steady state. Why does it shorten when the pump increases? 2. An atom has $\tau_{sp}=10$ ns at 500 nm. What is $\tau_{sp}$ of a transition with the same dipole moment at 10 µm? At 1 nm? 3. A He–Ne laser emits 1 mW in one mode. Estimate the power spontaneously emitted by the inverted Ne atoms into all other modes ($\Delta N_{th}\approx10^{15}$ m⁻³, tube volume 0.2 cm³, $\tau_{sp}=100$ ns). 4. Show that $R_{21}(\text{stim})/R_{21}(\text{spon})$ equals the number of photons in the mode.
